quizzes.title: Foundations Checkpoint
quizzes.description: Covers: Algorithms & Big-O, Arrays & Dynamic Lists, Stacks & Queues.

questions.prompt: Which running time grows the slowest as the input size n gets bigger (the best one)?
questions.explanation: O(1) is constant: the work does not grow at all. The order from best to worst is O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n^2).
The inner loop runs 3 times for each of the 4 outer rounds, so count is incremented 4 x 3 = 12 times.

questions.prompt: Why is my_list.insert(0, x) slow on a big list?
options: Every existing item has to shift one place to the right
Python must sort the list first
It copies the list to the hard disk
Index 0 is not allowed in a list
questions.explanation: Items sit side by side in memory, so making room at the front moves all n items. That costs O(n).

questions.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.append(4)
print(q.popleft(), q.pop())
questions.explanation: popleft() removes from the front (1) and pop() removes from the back (4).

questions.prompt: Fill in the method that pushes an item onto a list-based stack.
questions.explanation: append adds an item at the end of the list, which is the top of the stack. pop() later removes it.

quizzes.title: Linked Structures & Trees Checkpoint
quizzes.description: Covers: Linked Lists, Trees & Binary Search Trees, Hash Tables.

questions.prompt: In a singly linked list, what does the last node's next link hold?
questions.explanation: None marks the end of the list. A loop like while current is not None stops there.

questions.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
        self.next = None

a = Node(1)
b = Node(2)
c = Node(3)
a.next = b
b.next = c
print(a.next.next.v)
questions.explanation: a.next is b and b.next is c, so a.next.next is c, whose v is 3.

questions.prompt: In a binary search tree, where does a value smaller than the current node go?
options: Above the node as its parent
questions.explanation: BST rule: smaller values go left and bigger values go right.

questions.prompt: You insert 5, 3, 8, 1 into an empty BST, in that order. What does an inorder traversal give?
questions.explanation: Inorder (left, node, right) on a BST always gives the values in sorted order.
"pear" and "kiwi" both have length 4, and 4 % 4 is 0. Two keys in the same bucket is a collision.

quizzes.title: Algorithms Checkpoint
quizzes.description: Covers: Sorting & Searching, Graphs, BFS & DFS.

questions.prompt: What must be true before you can use binary search on a list?
questions.explanation: Binary search throws away half the list by comparing with the middle item. That only works if the list is in order.

questions.code:
data = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
low, high = 0, 4
mid = (low + high) // 2
print(data[mid])

questions.explanation: sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original list unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which search goes as deep as possible along one path before it backtracks?
questions.explanation: DFS follows one path to the end first, usually with recursion. BFS explores layer by layer.

questions.prompt: What is the running time of merge sort?
questions.explanation: The list is halved about log n times, and each level of merging does about n work, giving O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Fill in the deque method that takes the next vertex from the front of a BFS queue.
questions.code:
from collections import deque
queue = deque(["A", "B"])
v = queue.____()
print(v)
questions.explanation: popleft() removes and returns the first item in O(1). This gives BFS its first-in, first-out order.
